title.en: Parametric surface with a declared domain and degeneracies

summary: Build a surface from an explicit parameter domain and decide in advance what happens at poles, seams and collapsed edges.
objective: The surface renders without dark or flickering facets at its poles, apexes and seams, and the seam behaves exactly as the record declares it should.
intent_signals: build a surface from an equation
how many segments should this surface have
normals break at the tip of the cone
example_prompts: Build a torus knot surface from its equations and keep the seam invisible.
Show a surface of revolution whose profile touches the axis, and explain the tip.
Tessellate a saddle more densely where it curves fastest.
negative_signals: sculpt an organic character by hand
not_for: Meshes that arrive already triangulated from a scan, a CAD kernel or an asset file.
Implicit surfaces defined only by a scalar field, which need threshold-based extraction instead.

principles: The parameter domain is part of the object description. Record the u and v ranges, which parameters are periodic, and which boundary curves are seams to be closed rather than real open edges.

A parameterization only describes a surface normal where its two partial-derivative directions stay independent. Poles, cone apexes and collapsed profile ends are places where the surface still exists but the parameterization stops describing its orientation.
Sampling density belongs to the geometry of the surface, not to a single global slider. A uniform grid over a strongly non-uniform map spends triangles on flat regions and starves the tight ones.

Decide before building whether the result must be a closed boundary of a solid or may stay open. That decision drives seam welding, facing orientation and whether any volume-like reading of the object is meaningful.
implementation: Evaluate the position function over the declared domain and keep the u and v values with each sample, so texture placement, colour encoding and label anchoring can be recomputed later without re-deriving the map.

Take normals from the partial derivatives wherever they are independent. Where the cross product of the partials vanishes, distinguish the two cases: at a smooth pole a limiting normal usually exists and can be substituted, while at a genuine apex or crease no single normal exists and the record must choose per-face normals or another declared shading convention. Record the choice instead of letting a zero-length normal reach shading.

For a periodic parameter choose one of two documented treatments: duplicate the seam ring with identical positions and distinct texture coordinates, or weld the seam and accept a texture discontinuity. Do not leave the choice implicit.
Collapse a pole ring to one shared position only when the surface is genuinely a single point there. Otherwise keep the ring so the surrounding fan can carry different normals per triangle.
Refine adaptively: subdivide in the parameter where the normal turns more than a stated angle between neighbouring samples, and stop at a declared minimum edge length so the refinement terminates.
When the surface is a mathematical illustration, keep the defining formula, the domain and any restriction visible in the scene text so the viewer can tell the drawn extent from the full surface.
observable_checks: Under a moving light, the poles, apexes and seams show no black facets, no flicker and no visible crack at the largest camera zoom the scene allows.
The vertex count at a seam matches the declared treatment: a welded seam has one ring, a split seam has two coincident rings, and neither shows a gap when the object is scaled up.
A checkered parameter texture or wireframe overlay shows the intended parameter flow, with the denser bands where the record says curvature is highest.

Restricting the domain to D' renders exactly the image r(D'), checked against the defining map. Do not infer an area fraction from a parameter fraction; overlapping parameter values may represent the same retained surface.

creative_affordances: The parameter grid itself can become a visible design element: exposed isolines, ribbed construction or a deliberately coarse faceting are legitimate looks.
A degenerate point can be dramatised rather than hidden, for example as a pinched spire or a visible cap, as long as the record says which choice was made.
known_limits: This profile governs the parameterization and its degeneracies only. It does not establish that the chosen formula models any real object.
The regularity condition cited here is a definition from calculus, not a numerical robustness guarantee for a specific floating-point evaluation.
Authored reusable guidance; no runtime artifact or rendered result has been observed for this record.

claims.statement: A surface parameterization written as a vector function of two parameters is called regular, and the surface smooth, when the cross product of its two partial derivatives is nonzero for every parameter pair in the domain; where that cross product vanishes the parameterization supplies no normal direction.
claims.scope: Textbook definition of regularity and smoothness for a parameterized surface. It identifies where a parameterization degenerates; it does not say the underlying point set is defective, and it makes no statement about numerical conditioning near the degeneracy.
